title: Ryan Daniels on X: 'The White Collar Revolution is Here' — the Neofirm thesis, and the claim that professional-work quality has become measurable
author: Ryan Daniels

dom.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Daniels anticipates substantial automation and practitioner-engineer service models, which is consistent with the cluster’s premise that legal production will change. However, he does not address associate apprenticeship, expertise reproduction, the verification paradox, or deliberate replacement training, so his position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: As AI’s automation threshold increased, and as we discovered subtle ideas that could improve our lawyers’ and clients’ lives, we faced reality: we had to write our own code.
Teams made up of engineers and active practitioners have an unfair advantage here.

st.t: Legal economics: AI makes adoption a model problem
st.an: Daniels accepts that AI adoption requires business-model redesign and materially extends the proposition with a concrete “Neofirm” model: integrated practitioner-engineer teams, corporate structures supporting long-term R&D and equity, outcome-based pricing, continuous quality measurement, and direct development on LLMs. His claims about future quality transparency and agent-led services are predictions rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Corporate structures that encourage R&D investment and long term equity  1.
Business models that charge for outcomes instead of hours worked  1.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Daniels accepts that AI chiefly disrupts labour-based production and hourly economics while retaining practitioners within integrated service delivery. He materially extends the cluster by specifying a “Neofirm” model built around practitioner–engineer teams, long-term R&D capital, outcome pricing and measurable quality. His stronger predictions about agentic delivery and software–services convergence are forecasts rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: They are not selling human labor; instead they are selling the value that comes from better ways of working.

kp.k: Firm strategy must follow a moving automation frontier
kp.d: Daniels argues that attracting, training and retaining outstanding professionals is no longer a sufficient competitive strategy. He recommends continuously identifying what machines can perform, transferring that work to AI, and reorganising firms around research and invention as model capabilities improve. This is a strategic prescription rather than a measured finding about displacement.
qs: Today’s firms need to discover the frontier between minds and machines – what is automatable and what is uniquely human – and relentlessly offload any work beneath that threshold to AI.
Model capabilities keep improving so this is a moving target. Firms need to become dynamic centers of research and immense invention.

kp.k: Bessemer provides an analogy for services industrialisation
kp.d: Daniels compares professional services to steelmaking's transition from scarce, uneven artisanal production to fast, inexpensive, high-quality production following Bessemer's 1856 innovation. The proposed mechanism is organisational as well as technological: production businesses become research centres that continually improve their methods. This is historical analogy supporting his thesis, not direct evidence about legal services outcomes.
qs: This all changed in 1856. Henry Bessemer introduced a method to produce high quality steel, fast and cheap, using hot air and pig iron.
After Bessemer, mills became centers of research and discovery, inventing increasingly better methods of production.
Today, professional services firms are having their Bessemer steel moment.

kp.k: Neofirms combine practitioners, engineers, equity and outcome pricing
kp.d: Daniels presents the Neofirm as a replacement model for traditional professional partnerships, motivated by computers' ability to perform complex work previously reserved for attorneys, consultants and accountants. Its defining features are an equal practitioner–technical staffing split, corporate structures supporting research and long-term equity, outcome-based pricing, and systematic quality measurement. These are proposed organisational characteristics, not reported market-wide adoption figures.
qs: Computers can do complex knowledge work that was previously the exclusive domain of skilled attorneys, consultants or accountants.
An equal split of practitioners and engineers/AI researchers
Corporate structures that encourage R&D investment and long term equity
Business models that charge for outcomes instead of hours worked
Obsession over defining, measuring, and constantly improving quality

kp.k: Partnership distributions allegedly impede long-term technology investment
kp.d: Daniels asserts that America's top 100 law firms earned a combined $69 billion in profit in 2025, exceeding Google's 2025 R&D budget, and distributed every cent to partners. He argues that annual distributions and restrictions on outside equity weaken incentives for long-term investment, contrasting these with venture-funded corporations. The document supplies no supporting data source or jurisdictional qualification for these financial and legal assertions.
qs: America’s top 100 law firms made a combined $69 billion in profit in 2025, greater than Google’s 2025 R&D budget. Every cent was paid out to the firms’ partners as compensation.
Traditional firms are structured as partnerships that pay out profits every year as a dividend. They legally can’t sell equity to outsiders. They have little incentive to invest in the future.
Neofirms are corporations, able to raise venture capital and take risks with long term payoffs.

kp.k: Document pricing rewards sacrificing current revenue for automation
kp.d: Drawing on his work at Crosby, Daniels describes an actual resource-allocation tension between lawyers serving clients and experimenting with engineers. He reports billing by the document rather than the hour and prioritising long-term value over annual profits-per-partner. His example of an afternoon developing agent benchmarks potentially saving twenty days the following year illustrates expected future margin, not a documented realised saving.
qs: Every hour a lawyer spends experimenting with an engineer is time they could have spent working on a new client’s request.
But our goal is to increase long term value, not annual profits-per-partner. Plus, we bill by the document, not by the hour.
So when a Crosby lawyer spends an afternoon writing agent benchmarks, we know this could save us twenty days of her time next year, which creates future margin we can reinvest.

kp.k: Fixed-price incentives underpin a reusable-rocket analogy
kp.d: Daniels attributes SpaceX's innovation to a shift from cost-plus remuneration to fixed-price payment for results and uses this as an analogy for professional-service business models. He predicts that Neofirms across industries will develop comparably transformative reusable capabilities; the document does not present this as an observed legal-market outcome.
qs: SpaceX moved spacecraft development from a cost-plus model – where they got paid for each hour worked – to fixed price – where they got paid for results.
Aligning incentives spurred them to redefine what was possible, like building rockets that return to a launchpad.
Neofirms in every professional services industry will build their reusable rocket equivalent.

kp.k: Evaluations allegedly make professional-work quality measurable
kp.d: Daniels argues that AI researchers have recently converted subjective professional standards into objective evaluations and rubrics. He contrasts this with evidence-based medicine's rise in the 1980s, claiming that white-collar work previously lacked an equivalent because quality was difficult to measure. He proposes evaluating both human and agent output to accelerate improvement, but supplies no named evaluation, validation study or performance results.
qs: In the 1980s, the evidence-based medicine movement took off.
No similar movement took hold in white collar work because, unlike patient outcomes, work quality was notoriously hard to measure.
Over the past few years, AI researchers have learned to distill squishy subjective standards into rigorous, objective ones.
At Neofirms, expert professionals and researchers design evaluations to measure the output of all work, human or agent; this creates a tight feedback loop that helps rapidly improve quality.

kp.k: Benchmarks could reshape selection without eliminating elite partners
kp.d: Daniels predicts that clients will increasingly select professionals using demonstrated performance rather than educational pedigree or firm prestige. He also predicts greater value for elite partners supported by agents, while explicitly acknowledging that reputation and some professional contributions cannot be quantified. The $3,000/hour versus $1,000/hour comparison illustrates his anticipated ability to distinguish quality, not an empirical pricing result.
qs: Instead of choosing your banker based on their alma mater or firm prestige, you will ask to see their benchmarks.
Neofirms will make elite partners even more valuable, leveraging them with armies of agents.
Nor does it mean that everything top lawyers or consultants do can be quantified. Sometimes you are paying for reputation.
Even still, as more tasks become measurable with evals, you will be able to choose between a $3,000/hour partner and a $1,000/hour partner and actually know the difference.

kp.k: Practitioner-engineer teams build proprietary tools from client experience
kp.d: Daniels argues that easier software creation makes deciding what to build the central advantage, favouring teams combining engineers with practitioners working directly with clients. As first-person evidence, he reports that Crosby tried off-the-shelf legal AI tools, found none fully suitable, and began writing its own code as automation capabilities and identified opportunities expanded. He generalises this into a Neofirm model of building directly on LLMs rather than relying on SaaS vendors.
qs: As software gets easier to write, the thing that matters most is deciding what to build.
Teams made up of engineers and active practitioners have an unfair advantage here.
We piloted every off-the-shelf legal AI tool we could, but nothing was perfect.
As AI’s automation threshold increased, and as we discovered subtle ideas that could improve our lawyers’ and clients’ lives, we faced reality: we had to write our own code.
Neofirms don’t buy SaaS or opinionated wrappers. They don’t request features from vendors.

kp.k: Software-service convergence promises qualitatively different client experiences
kp.d: Daniels predicts that software and services businesses will eventually become indistinguishable. His illustrative trajectory moves from accountants supplying request ETAs and retaining detailed business context to tax advisers predicting audits with certainty, insurance policies changing with codebases, and lawyers' agents negotiating directly with counterparties' agents to remove months of redlining. These are forward-looking scenarios with only the imprecise horizons of 'over time' and 'soon'.
qs: Over time, the distinction between software and services companies will disappear.
For now, this might look like your accountant giving you an ETA on every request and remembering astonishingly nuanced context about your business and customers.
Soon, your tax advisor will predict, with certainty, that you will get audited.
Your insurance broker will dynamically change your policies based on your codebase.
And your lawyer’s agents will negotiate with your counterparty’s agents, to eliminate months of contract redlining.

kp.k: New incentives aim to overcome professional resistance
kp.d: Daniels asserts that professional services rank behind code generation in suitability for LLMs because they involve large volumes of unstructured qualitative text. He identifies a tension between this technical suitability and professionals' aversion to change, which he links to clients' demand for stability and risk mitigation. He argues that pairing experts with researchers and rewarding task transfer to AI resolves this tension; the ranking and organisational effect are assertions without supporting comparative results.
qs: LLMs are best suited for jobs that contain huge volumes of unstructured, qualitative text. Code generation ranks first, but professional services work ranks second.
Stability and risk mitigation are major parts of the value they provide to their clients.
But it means that, while software developers get rewarded for adopting new technologies fast, white collar workers get penalized.
They pair subject matter experts with cutting edge researchers to take full advantage of the AI era.
Their business model encourages practitioners to hand off tasks beneath the automation threshold, instead of clinging to old ways of working.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Daniels claims AI makes a talent-centred professional-services model insufficient for survival and requires continuously shifting work from humans to machines.
pts.d: Daniels argues that computers already perform complex work previously reserved for attorneys, consultants and accountants. In his account, firms must identify a moving automation threshold, offload work below it to AI and become organisations devoted to research and invention. He frames this as a structural transformation already underway, rather than simply adopting tools to make existing professionals faster.

pts.k: Daniels predicts that practitioner–engineer 'Neofirms' will replace traditional professional-services firms.
pts.d: He defines Neofirms by equal numbers of practitioners and engineers/AI researchers, corporate structures supporting long-term equity and R&D, outcome-based charging and systematic quality measurement. He contrasts this with his characterisation of traditional partnerships as hourly-billing organisations designed to retain professionals rather than experiment. These are claims about firms delivering professional services, not merely software vendors.

pts.k: Daniels argues that corporate ownership and non-hourly pricing turn automation and R&D into long-term profit opportunities.
pts.d: He claims annual partner distributions and restrictions on outside equity discourage traditional firms from investing for the future, whereas corporations can raise venture capital and accept near-term revenue losses for future returns. At Crosby, he reports billing by the document and allocating lawyer time to engineering and agent benchmarks. He presents resulting time savings and reinvestable margins as the incentive for innovation, not as demonstrated financial outcomes.

pts.k: Daniels claims AI evaluation methods have made previously subjective professional-work quality measurable and will change how clients select providers.
pts.d: He says researchers can translate subjective standards into objective evaluations and rubrics. He describes Neofirms as applying these methods to both human and agent output, generating feedback that improves quality. He predicts clients will ask for benchmarks rather than rely primarily on educational credentials or firm prestige, and will be able to distinguish the quality associated with different partner prices. He qualifies this by acknowledging that some work and reputation cannot be quantified. His claim concerns evaluation and benchmarking, not a specified process for human verification of AI output.

pts.k: Daniels predicts increased value for elite partners through agent-supported work, alongside automation of tasks below the capability threshold.
pts.d: His thesis is not that professional experience becomes irrelevant. He predicts elite partners will become more valuable by working with large numbers of agents. This combines augmentation of senior expertise with substitution of AI for automatable tasks. He does not specify associate headcounts, staffing shapes, promotion models or the human supervision arrangements for those agents.

pts.k: Daniels predicts practitioner-led proprietary development will outperform reliance on packaged software and blur the boundary between software and services.
pts.d: He argues that easier software development shifts the main advantage toward knowing what to build. Teams combining active practitioners with engineers can discover needs through real client work and iterate quickly. He portrays Neofirms as building directly on LLMs rather than depending on packaged SaaS or vendor feature requests, and predicts these teams will create leading technology over the next decade.

pts.k: Daniels forecasts qualitatively different client services, including agent-to-agent contract negotiation that removes months of redlining.
pts.d: For legal services, he predicts opposing parties' agents will negotiate with each other. In adjacent professional services, he envisages accountants supplying request completion estimates and retaining detailed business context, tax advisers predicting audits with certainty, and insurance brokers dynamically adjusting policies using clients' codebases. These are service scenarios and predictions, not reported deployments or measured results.

pts.k: Daniels claims Neofirms resolve a mismatch between professional services' suitability for LLMs and practitioners' incentives to resist rapid change.
pts.d: He ranks professional-services work second to code generation in suitability for LLMs because of its large volumes of unstructured qualitative text. He argues that professionals provide stability and risk mitigation and therefore face penalties for rapid adoption, unlike software developers. Pairing domain experts with researchers and rewarding task automation is his proposed organisational solution.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The argument draws on Daniels's Crosby experience, an uncited financial comparison and historical analogies; it supplies no named evaluation results or measured market-replacement outcomes.
pts.d: Daniels reports Crosby's document pricing, lawyer–engineer collaboration, allocation disputes and trials of off-the-shelf legal AI tools as first-hand experience. His example of saving twenty lawyer-days next year is a prospective possibility, not an observed saving. He states that the top 100 US law firms earned $69 billion in 2025 profits, all distributed to partners, and compares this with Google's R&D budget without identifying a source. He invokes Bessemer steelmaking, SpaceX's pricing incentives and evidence-based medicine as analogies for R&D-driven transformation. His reference to Charlie Munger supports his incentives argument by quoted authority rather than supplying empirical evidence. Although evaluation is central to the thesis, the document provides no named benchmarks, rubrics, scores, research studies or comparative quality data. The post also promotes Crosby's services.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2026 source describes transformation as already underway, while leaving most forecasts undated or expressed as 'soon', 'over time' or within the next decade.
pts.d: Daniels places advances in quality evaluation over the preceding few years and presents complex-work automation as a current capability. His financial comparison concerns 2025. The Crosby time-saving illustration concerns the following year; leadership in technology is forecast for the next decade. Agent negotiation and the other advanced service scenarios receive no precise deployment dates. The mechanism depends on continuing model improvements, identifying tasks below a moving automation threshold, investing practitioner time in R&D, and adopting incentives that capture automation gains. He explicitly limits claims of measurability by preserving a role for experience and reputation. His statement about traditional firms' inability to sell outside equity is not accompanied by jurisdictional qualifications.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes affect professional-services providers, practitioners, engineers, investors, software vendors and clients.
pts.d: Traditional law firms, accounting firms, consultancies, banks and insurance brokerages face restructuring or replacement in Daniels's account. Neofirms gain a competitive position by delivering services through proprietary technology. Practitioners give up some billable client time for R&D and hand automatable tasks to AI; elite partners are predicted to gain value through agent support. Engineers and AI researchers become core colleagues in equal-number teams. Outside investors can finance long-term development in the proposed corporate model. Packaged software vendors become less central as providers build their own systems. Clients are promised more demonstrable quality, better-informed provider selection and new service experiences, including shorter contract negotiations. The document does not separately predict effects on junior hiring, individual access to justice or unmet civil legal need.
